terms.definition: Cash the GP demands from LPs to fund investments and fees. Cumulative capital calls = Paid-In Capital (PIC).
GP's profit share, commonly ~20% of profits above a preferred return; the main driver of gross-to-net drag between fund IRR and LP net return.
Total capital an LP contractually promises to a fund. Not paid up front; called in tranches over the investment period.
Cumulative distributions divided by paid-in capital. The realized, cash-on-cash multiple — permanent unless distributions are recallable.
The IRR of the index-future-valued cash-flow stream (each flow compounded to T by the index return). The annualized excess return (alpha) over the benchmark. α > 0 = outperformance.
Cash or stock returned to LPs from realizations, dividends, or recapitalizations.
Gross is before management fees, fund expenses, and carried interest; net is after. LPs care about net. A GP leading with gross is a tell.
The minimum LP return (often ~8% per year) that must be achieved before the GP earns carried interest.

terms.term: IRR (Internal Rate of Return, since-inception SI-IRR)
terms.definition: The money-weighted annualized discount rate that sets the net present value of all fund cash flows (including terminal NAV as a final inflow) to zero. GIPS-required headline return for closed-end funds.

The early-life dip in net IRR and TVPI below par — caused by management fees, fund expenses, and investments still held at cost — before value creation and exits lift returns. Plotting net value over time traces a 'J.'

Index-discounted (distributions + NAV) divided by index-discounted contributions. A wealth ratio: >1 beats the market, =1 matches, <1 underperforms. 1.20 = 20% more terminal wealth than an identically-timed index investment.

The original PME (1996). Builds a synthetic index portfolio that buys on capital calls and sells on distributions, producing a PME IRR and IRR spread. Breaks (negative synthetic NAV) on strong outperformers — the 'shortness problem.'
IRR variant that assumes an explicit, separate reinvestment rate for interim distributions. Addresses IRR's reinvestment assumption flaw but is rarely the industry headline.
Total value divided by invested capital. Most precisely used at the deal level and gross of fund fees. Net fund MOIC ≈ TVPI.

Proprietary CA fix for the LN shortness problem. Each distribution sells the same proportion of the synthetic portfolio as the fund distributed of its own value — keeping the synthetic NAV always positive. Difference between fund return and mPME return is reported as 'Value-Add' in basis points.
The GP's fair-value estimate of the unrealized portfolio at a valuation date. An estimate, not cash — the soft, manipulable input in any metric that uses it.

Fund-level loan secured by the portfolio assets. Debt-funded distributions inflate DPI and IRR while leaving TVPI ~flat pre-interest (and reducing it after interest). Distributions are often recallable.
Cumulative capital actually called from LPs. The denominator of DPI, RVPI, and TVPI.
PIC divided by total commitment. Measures how much of the LP's pledge has been drawn.
A family of methods comparing a private fund's performance to a public index on the fund's own cash-flow timing. Answers whether the illiquid fund beat the liquid alternative.

Scales all fund distributions by a single factor lambda (λ) chosen so the synthetic public NAV exactly equals the private NAV at terminal date, guaranteeing a positive (non-short) result. Invented to fix the LN shortness problem.
A single IRR computed on the combined cash flows of many funds; capital-weighted, so large funds dominate. Cambridge Associates uses a pooled horizon IRR as its official benchmark figure.

Rank within a vintage-year, same-strategy cohort. Top quartile = best 25%, by a specified metric (IRR or TVPI) at a specific provider. The same fund can be in different quartiles depending on metric, provider, vintage definition, and strategy cut.
The distinction between DPI from genuine exits (permanent, costless) and DPI from recallable NAV-loan proceeds (borrowed, reversible, interest-bearing). Not all DPI is equally trustworthy.
A distribution the GP can claw back — e.g., to repay a NAV loan or for recycling. Recallable distributions should not be treated as permanent DPI.
NAV divided by paid-in capital. The unrealized, paper multiple — the GP's estimate of what the portfolio is still worth per dollar called.

A revolving credit facility secured by LPs' uncalled commitments. Delays LP capital calls, shortening the period LP cash is outstanding and mechanically raising IRR. MOIC/TVPI is ~unchanged (slightly reduced by interest). ILPA 2020 guidance requires IRR disclosure with and without the facility.
(Distributions + NAV) divided by paid-in capital. TVPI = DPI + RVPI by construction. The total value multiple, usually reported net of fees and carry.
Fund return minus mPME return, expressed in basis points. Cambridge's proprietary market-adjusted performance measure.

The cohort year of a fund, used as the basis for peer benchmarking. Defined inconsistently across providers as first capital call, first close, or final close — a fund near a year boundary can land in different quartiles at different providers.

The difference between gross IRR/MOIC and net IRR/TVPI. Equal to the cost of management fees, fund expenses, and carried interest borne by the LP — typically several hundred basis points on IRR and a few tenths of a turn on MOIC for a 2-and-20 fund.

The failure mode of the original LN/ICM method: if a fund strongly outperforms, its large distributions require selling more index than the synthetic portfolio holds, driving the synthetic NAV negative. The PME IRR becomes incalculable. Fixed by mPME or PME+.
Fund IRR minus the Long–Nickels PME IRR. A negative spread means the fund underperformed the index on its own cash-flow schedule.

The distortion that occurs when datasets exclude funds that closed or stopped reporting, leaving only survivors (typically stronger performers). Burgiss/MSCI Private Capital is considered survivorship-bias-free within its LP-reporting population.

LP-reported private equity dataset with data back to 1978, covering 13,000+ funds and ~$15tn cumulative at the time of MSCI's acquisition (completed October 2023). Considered the research gold standard for cash-flow data; underpins the PERC academic dataset.

The most widely quoted consultant PE benchmark, sourced from fund financial statements and GP/advisory-client relationships. Uses a pooled horizon IRR and proprietary mPME. Academic sources note a possible tilt toward GPs actively raising new funds.
